free-homestead.subject: Free Homestead
free-homestead.location_scope: Southeastern Nebraska; a reconstructed homestead cabin based on the Palmer-Epard building type
documented_features: Palmer built a 14-by-16-foot mixed-hardwood cabin in 1867. A rear lean-to was added only in 1875-1880 [S1].
The NPS account identifies homemade brick and lime mortar alongside hardwoods, and occupation from spring 1868 [S2].

Modern photographs show hewn horizontal logs, pale chinking, notched corners, a steep gable, brick-filled timber gable framing and small glazed windows. The 2024 restoration replaced damaged logs, so photographs are construction references, not untouched 1867 fabric [S3].
documented_colors: Brown to gray unpainted wood, red-brown brick and pale mortar are visible in the restoration photograph [S3]. Exact original colours are not measured; render natural materials at full strength, with green cultivated ground rather than invented paint.
free-homestead.render_brief: A compact unoccupied Nebraska homestead cabin, representing 1868-1874 before a later rear addition. Rectangular 14-by-16-foot footprint, one principal room, irregular hewn horizontal hardwood logs with notched corners and broad pale chinking. A steep dark wooden shingle gable roof shelters a warm red-brown brick-and-timber gable infill. Give the long wall one plain plank entrance; small multi-pane glazed windows break the otherwise solid log walls, with a smaller loft window in the gable. Natural wood, cream mortar and red brick remain distinct in clear warm light. A narrow bare-earth approach meets green grass and the edge of a small cultivated patch. Complete all four walls. No porch, rear lean-to, modern concrete pad, paved path, utility lines, restoration equipment, signs, people or invented paint. This is a carefully disclosed reconstruction of a homestead type; the restored museum cabin informs construction but is not presented as an exact untouched 1868 appearance.
free-homestead.history_lesson: George Palmer built his Nebraska cabin in 1867 and moved in with his family the next spring. A home and land improvements formed part of proving a homestead claim; the miniature reconstructs this dwelling type.

sources.title: NPS — Palmer-Epard Cabin
sources.supports: Construction date, dimensions, mixed hardwoods, later lean-to, and repeated twentieth-century relocation and rehabilitation. Modern fog photograph supports overall silhouette only.

sources.title: NPS — Brief History of the Palmer-Epard Cabin, transcript
sources.supports: Homemade brick in lime mortar, hardwood species, occupation in 1868, cultivation and improvements involved in proving the claim. Does not specify each opening or gable's original arrangement.

sources.title: NPS — Palmer-Epard restoration, December 19, 2024
sources.supports: Restoration used matching local logs and period-style tool marks. Attached colour photograph supports the current log, mortar, brick-gable and window forms; it also demonstrates that the visible building contains modern repairs.

uncertainties: Opening placement, original roof and gable details, chinking condition and landscaping are reconstruction informed by a repeatedly restored building. No claim of an exact 1868 replica.
The original foundation is not established here: conceal it at earth level rather than copying the modern concrete base.
The two NPS narratives differ on the precise May 1875 patent date; this brief makes no day-specific claim.
free-homestead.visual_source_review: Viewed the actual NPS fog and 2024 restoration photos locally before authoring: /tmp/oldwest-free-homestead-reference.jpg and /tmp/oldwest-free-homestead-restoration.jpg. Modern workers, tools, hardscape and infrastructure are excluded.
